name: V-taper / shoulder-to-waist ratio

lead: A V-taper is a torso that is wide at the shoulders and upper back and narrows to a small waist. In bodybuilding it is a classic ideal, and in looksmaxxing it is a standard frame goal often written as a shoulder-to-waist ratio.
A figure of about 1.6, tied to the golden ratio, is commonly cited as the target. Community members discuss how to approach it through delt and lat training and fat loss.

paras: The ratio rises when the shoulders and upper back get wider or the waist gets smaller. Wider means deltoid and latissimus muscle growth on top of the bone structure set by the clavicles. Smaller waist is mainly linked to body fat loss; abdominal exercise on its own is described as insufficient for reducing waist girth.

The practice itself is ordinary training and dieting. Reported concerns are mostly about body-image fixation and about skipping legs or overtraining while chasing a number. The 1.6 target is a cultural convention, and the research behind it is thin.

lead: The V-taper is a physique in which broad shoulders and a wide upper back narrow down to a slim waist, giving an inverted-triangle silhouette. It is a long-standing ideal in bodybuilding and is discussed in looksmaxxing as the shoulder-to-waist ratio [1].

A figure of about 1.6, linked to the golden ratio, is often stated as the target. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, attributes this to bodybuilding aesthetics and credits figures such as Steve Reeves and Arnold Schwarzenegger with popularizing the look, although several of its citations for the attractiveness claims do not appear to match those claims [1][2].

Wikipedia's article on waist-hip ratio, which is about attractiveness research, reports one study in which the waist-to-chest ratio was the largest determinant of male attractiveness, and does not discuss shoulder-to-waist ratio itself [3]. No clinical studies of the ratio as a target were found.
infobox: Shoulder width divided by waist width

paras: Grokipedia describes the V-taper as being built from the deltoids, latissimus dorsi and trapezius on a skeletal base set by clavicle length, with a narrower waist coming from low body fat and limited oblique bulk [1]. These anatomical claims are consistent with Wikipedia's description of the deltoid and clavicle, though the ratio targets themselves are not defined there [4][5].

Grokipedia credits mid-twentieth century classic physiques, notably Steve Reeves, and the 1970s Golden Era with making the V-taper a standard ideal [1]. This history comes from an AI-generated source and has not been checked against primary histories here.

In looksmaxxing, the ratio is a frame metric. Proponents say a high ratio signals masculinity, strength and health, and they discuss training the shoulders, back and neck while keeping the waist small. Waist size is said to depend mainly on fat loss, and Wikipedia's abdominal exercise entry notes that a 2011 study found abdominal exercise alone does not reduce abdominal fat or girth [6].

The sources reviewed contain one relevant finding, that waist-to-chest ratio was reported as the largest determinant of male attractiveness in a study summarized on Wikipedia [3]. Grokipedia states that broad shoulders paired with a narrow waist signal dominance and that upper-body strength cues account for most variance in men's bodily attractiveness, but supplies no sample sizes or methods and cites weak sources [1].
No studies found. Research on body shape and attractiveness exists but does not test whether pursuing a 1.6 ratio changes outcomes.

lore.intro: The V-taper is discussed as a core body goal, with the ratio often posted and compared, and with arguments over whether leg training harms the ratio [2].

claims.claim: A shoulder-to-waist ratio of about 1.6 is the ideal.
A narrow waist comes from fat loss, not abdominal exercise.
Broad shoulders with a narrow waist signal dominance and attractiveness.
